In accordance with the decrees of the Government, all the Jesuit establisltments throughout France were closed at an early Mum on Wednesday morning. The Jesuits protected, but offered en reeimance, though I. some instances they insisted upon being led out of their domiciles to prove thst they left end...avulsion. The Jesuits of Lyons and Grenoble have given notice to the authorities of the inten- tion to tern then frauruities into lay societies, and ths question thus raised is to he settled in the law musts. .....

New Yo, Tneeday.—The excursion steamboat Seaman- hake, with 300 passengers on board, has been burned off College Point, Long 'inland Sound, near New York. It in estimated that fifty persons were either burned to death or dtownel.
The bodies which !lave been recovered have been con- veyed Co the Morgue, where they have been identified !during the day by the relatives and fri.nda of the deceased. THE BERLIN CONFERENCE.

...... .... Baratta, Monday.-- he conference at its sitting to-day unanimously approved thefts, draft of adocument, prepared by the French ambassador embodying its definite decision in respect to the Greek frontier. The New Greek frontier lino as finally established by the conference commences on the east at the month of the river Maurelongos, and passes thence over the highest peaks of the Olympus and Find... ranges. At Kanhalbacki it strikes the river Nalimis,whose course it follows to its mouth. Turkey retains the Zaori distrkt. The conference afterwarda disposed of some of the secondary quest Mns which demand its attention, such as the ensuring of freedom of worship in the territories assigned to Greece, the settlement of the clahns of Mussulman land- owners who may prefer to emigrate rather than crane under Greek rule, and further, the amm.nt of the Turkish debt to be transferred to the Hellenic Government. All these questions were arranged in accordance with the stipule- tines of the Treaty of Berlin. Another subject of discus., sion was the question of frontier police and navigation regu- 1111011P.

--firTittesday the Conference met for the sixth time, the object being to sobmit the Protocol to a final revision. • ! Berlin Correspondent says that in the reasons which the Plenipotentiaries will assign for the decision at which they have arrived, special emphasis will be laid upon the fact I that the Conference desired to give strategical advantages to neither of the Powers directly interested, end that in determining the north-meet frontier, the chief object was to avoid future causes of trouble between the Albanians and the Greeks.
Thornilay.—The Conference met this afternoon at four o'clock, and remained in mmion until half-pant flee.

Mr. Gochen hen rel.,. rated with the Porte on the assiatance which it has rentleod to the Albanian League. The Sultan has asked lore copy, in Turkish, of Sir It Layard's memorable despatch—the last he wrote—to Earl Granville before leaving Constantinople. Some revelatioios were made at tile meet- ing of the Present Board of Guardiatia, at the Whiaton Workhouee, on Thureday last. The eerenity of the Guardians has frequently been interfered with during the last two yeses by malpractices of officialdom and the disclosures we print to day will awaken in the ratepayers no littlo astoniedareect the character of the discrepancies which have come to . light. Diseiciafied with a few ionall matters in con- ! neetion with the Workh our, the Guardia. deputed • acme of their number to " take etock " at the Works boa., and the report of the result of that inveatigation, presented at the fortnigatly meeting of the Board on Thursday, is a dfolaratiou of s condition of affairs that puts the management of the house in • very serious position. For this etnite of things Mr. Davi., the Master of the Werkha.e, was called before the Board to answer. The brandy and gin found in the house were declared to he abominably diluted, but the Master could nut account for their being so much under proof. lie was equally ignorant of what hilid become of the permits, but a Guardian supplied the knowledge by announcing that they had be n burnt. Brandy had been mined with port wine, and whilet there ought to hare been four and a half pints of the latter liquor in stock it had vanished, and no one could any how. Nearly a ton of mutton and beef —2,222iba. —had disappeered, but in what shape the Guardians were at a loss to divine. The Kanter en- deavoured to peremade the Board that tha other officers of the house had acquired most ravenous appstitee, to appease which he had served out to eat: i 2lbs. more a. week than the .ual rations, distribution of Roth which he bad never accounted for in his reckouings. Or rather, his clerk had not taken credit for cheer extrae in the redraftinge made on his behalf. The clerk we suspected of having eut up the meat under the Mas.r's superia - tendency, bat Mr. Mealowe, • Guardian, volunteered an opinion that the Mast r had superintended nothing. One of the Guardians ventured an opinion that the meat had been pat in such placer that any hungry mortal, if ao mit.deol, could have run off with a junk, and lessened the stock and another eagacione Gears dian of the ratepayer.' inter.ts had a notion that the "fashionable" eon.rts at the Workhouse in the , winter months of last year were ,dliad with hospitality, and that the festive board was graced with mewled . jeints that were "polished off " ad lihtnom. l'here . was • deficiency of 271 eggs, and for the disappearance of these from the stores the Master put in the plea that a great many had ones had been thrown away , and not aecounted for. The flour account wee said to , be correct throe creche ago, but, on the committee I overhauling the sacks of Sour, they found aix and a ,

half packs defifient. The Maetor's clerk am credited by the Master with blundering In the flour account, ha not having charged for four and • half rooke in the December quarter, and another four and a half packe in the Marell quarter. Ilow the fl.;ur actmunt CAMS tube right three week. RR°. and wrong at the time of , the committee'e inquiry, wee og cleared up and that subject was abaudoued to find Oct where 202 yard. a flannel had been transferred th The Mester, how over, was in total ignorance, "or, the books had not been made up." Tiew various deficienoes rear rid to represent a value of Lot 12, 4d., but alas delis- gummier; did not end hetet Mr. Meadows sad that I. March last the Muter wired for 2,000 yards of oldie% and he wanted to know why that was done when there were actually 1,500 yards in stock ; but the Master woo mum. The inventory book, it was said, had be ignored for two yin,., sod the other books were chats°. terited se deceptions. The Chairman hazarded as suer - that one of the ward, ia the house had not been viaitad by the Mwter for indie than a month, notwithstanding that he lived on the spot and the Master gave the quardi.ins to .ndaegand that piing up stairs freimently was tot in his line. but visiting' the manly down stairs was. Ile generally contrived. get through the house otice week, and if any- thing went wrong he depended on the nurses Ana porter putting him on the ler rive. Mr. liarrimu thought that if the Maeter had gone through the house daily it would not have exhaumed and he ww uickel enough to remark that the Master Wan sharp enough to have everything in apple pie order when the Visiting Conintittee came round." It trenimired that when the inviwtigdting committee was testing the aboininatily diluted braidiv ori gin, hunting after [henna:dug wt. and tryinz to find the toii of beef, lbw I eggs, the nra on a hitt packs ot dour, :awl the big roll of flannel, the !dank/ Itaa inhaling cie ralubrious at. mosphere of %kidney. Seeing th.t the bum-diens were in an angry retool the Master came to the conclusion that he had had a lease. that day not to trust too much to others. Its confessed that he felt his idisition very much, sad con- sidered that in the future he could Malta all to ltet through the house regularly. I'M; Chairman. [tonere, whilst he ex- tolled the matron condemned the Master Lir riermitting ex- travagance to run riot. Seeing that the (Mardians thaw wives had not taken stock for two years, and that the Masts, though he hal been ntock-takerat the ficiwnlow Workhoutm had not taken stock either, several of tile tivardians were honest enough to ekhlbla that l'a.y tot themselves Leen remiss in not exerclsiu; mere surveillance, arid, a a con- sequence, pleaded for the Mester to be given another ' "chance." HELENS CRICKET CLEW Sir,--Permit me to draw your attt-ntion to the latter part of the paragraph (which affects too persmally, as chairman) in your " Local Notes " of Saturday lASI rcsiwcting the St. , Helens Cricket Club. There are three m I 71,...1.111..1 v. '- 1. That the resignation wee accepted by a very narrow majority. The fact was that it was unanimously accepted. 2. That the chairman gave two casting vote.. He gave a casting vote on one occasion only. It. That the chairman elected himself to the post I was duly and unanimously elected to the position I oecupial by the committee. I think when your correspondent "Merno " criticism the actions of a hody of men he ought to take the trouble to ascertain the ACIIIAI facts, and not publish public-house gossip. ilOwn/a.—Before Mr, .;olkn Bratirit icluirn..) and

_ Henry Reynolds. A Dortmen BIIPROILATIL—John Burke, a red headed, {Powerful looking fellow. who h only been out of gaol& few days,was charged with being drunk atal disorderly in Mersey. street, on the 28th ult.—Sergeant !landlord said hot on Saturday night, about half.post nine, he etw the prieoner come out ol a house, and he waa gripped, and cursed and aware. Ile was aleo drunk., and etruck h father.—When charged by the magistrate.' clerk, the ',Heeler did not deny that he was guilty, but said hill father had struck hint with a hatchet. He was /lent to gaol one month, with hard labour. —Susannah Giblin, for being drunk and disorderly in Mersey- street, on the 26th April, and who had been apprehended on & warrant, was lined 10s. and cos., 16e. At, or in de...tilt of payment. 14 days' inaprioonment. ALLEGED CIAUNLIT TO A HOlVlR.—Thomas Huxley, an elderly man, who said he had been employed on boate About 00 years, was charged with cruelly illdresting a horse by working it in set unfit state, at Aston-by-Nutton, on the 17th Hilbert and Jackson gave evidence an to the condition of the animal, but as defendant aairl that See. grunt Dairciel, of Weston, and other officers bad seen it on the day of the allegul uffmce, and could prove that Blear not in the ntate described, the Bench said they would adjourn the hearing of the summons until the following Monday. BOYS STEALING Inox.—A SAO Csan.—Two respectably dresaed bons, named Win Frederick Hankinson and Richard Albert Robinson, both ot Spriugrstreet, were oh aged with stealing 201ba. of iron, the proporty of Mr. Philip Speakman. —Sergeant !landlord stated that on Viledneulay night, about half-past seven, he was going over the Big Pool Bridge, in the directinn of Mr. Speaknmn's boat yard. when he met the two boys. Hankinson was carrying a bag, and he stoppwl him; the other lad managed h, escape. He asked flankineon what he had in the bag, and he raid, Nothing but greet" but on examining it, be found it contained the iron produced. He asked hiin where they got the iron, and he replied out of Mr. Speakman's yard, end they had hod it hidden in some corn which was growing near that place Mlle@ the time they stole it. flankinson aided that he did not fetch the iron out of the yard, bet received it from the other boy, through a hole in the boards. The lad pointed out to him where the hole was, and he picked up the pieces of iron now produced near to the apot.—The boys admitted their guilt when formally charged.—Mr. Brundrit said it mono very nod thing to see two lads of such • tender age brought before the Bencli woo charge of theft, and it promised re,' badly for their future careers in life. The Bench were of opinion that perhapa the beg thing which could have been done in the case would hare been to order each of the prisoners to be well birched, hut thin time they would not make such on order, hut leave it to the parents to indict what punishment they considered needful. Mr. Brundrit then made some remarks criticising the mode in which the parent mug, judging from the reaults, have trained their children, and expressed a hope that they would keep a stricter watch ever them in future. Each of the parents would bare to pay a tins of 2s. dd. and las. coots.

A BATCH OF lintisenanos.—The following were fined 55. and costs for drunkenness mma Putman, Jam's Burns, , Mary. Burns, Daniel Farrel], and Jobn Mollarky. The eases were proved by Sergeant Eastlism. and F.C.'s Ross, Clarkson, and Thompson.—The man Farrell said he had been illuswl lay ono of the officers, and asks.' to take out a summons agaiest him.—The Inspector said be had inquired into the man's charge, which he considered to be utterly groun less. —Mr Hall told Farrell that he We at liberty to take what course he thought proper in the matter. Before Mr. 11•11 and Mr. F. 11. Gossage. . •

A BAD CASE.—Joseph Connolly, 12 years of age, concerm ing whom the Inspector said he had caused the police much trouble, was ordered tow imprimmed one doy and to be given etcstrokos with n birch rod, for stealing a sovereign, the money of Mr. Jonas Foster, limo merchant.—lt appeared from the statement of Mr. J. B Foulkes, clerk in the employ of Mr. Foster, that on the previous Friday the lad went to the offio, sod asked for 2e, which were due to his mother. He took & sovereign out of a 1.. a in one of the office drawers, for the purpose of gett Mg change, and left another sovereign in the drawer. He asked the prisoner to remain in the office whilst he was away. flower not absent more than two minutes, and whilst on his way hock he not the prisoner, and gave him the 2.5. On entering the office he looked in the drawer and missed the sovereign, ou which he wont to do prieoner'e bonne, and °barged him with stealing it, but he denied all knowledge r.f the affair. Wercersosr.—liefore Mr, Grrge Pilkington. • • ••• " - -

Sir:moon, Nicholson, and the Inepector. Dien:Rely° nig PEACY..—An old woman named Margaret Bell war eummoned for earning a breach of the peace, on the 17th ult. Sergeant N. est stated that at a quarter to one o'clock M the morning, whilst at the police office, he heard a great noise in Midwood.street, ander] going there found the defendant sweariug and misconducting herself in other ways. The erperintentlent of pollee arid there were four previous convictions against the defendant. She was ordered Concoct into sureties of £lO each, and one surety in £5 to keep the peace for three numthe, or, in default, be imprisoned 14 days. THVAPASPRI. - . This old adage, gemoilly applied to love-making, may, with equal truth, be applicable to naturalists, who are most im- politely descrimd by l',,yorh as stone-breakern, butterfly- catchers, and Bawer hunters. Well, never mind! On Saturday lvet, the AiKIVB society were determined to have an o outing," by way of a change, se they selected thc classical grounds of Hewlett for their day's exploration. A strange misunderstanding, however, occurred. slsny friends were led to think the train left Cl 2-15 pm., whilst a goodly num- bee left by the 1-311 p.m. express by way of Chester. When they reached the old city they had the mortification to see the train for llooton gently gliding away from the platform, just as they reached the spot. Hallooing proved useless, hut luckily they were shortly afterwards rent on tlwir trip by a special train. Truly they could not have been more highly favoured, had they claimed relationship with royalty itself; so in due time, without any more mishaps, they reached Hootrin. Wandering along a pleasant shady lane, where several gond plants were gatheriel, and explained, they shortly reached the hall belonging to R. A. Naylor, Esq. Here the gardener very obligingly conducted the party through the fruit and cool houses, and over stevefal other parlu of the ground. Fruits, chietiy grapes, cherries, and strawberries, were in perfection, and well grown, but these had not an much attraction as the forcing how, which con- tained A host of beautiful Gloxinias, Allatnandaxand strange looking Begoeies. In,, hardy feruery were ionic d most of our lirltieh ferns, together with very fine plants of the elegant Woodwardia. The open ground., as was interest- ingly painted oat by our conductor, had nuffered severely during the late severe winter. Immense tufts of the lovely pampaa gram, were killed by the frost, so an to leave a brown withered mass of foliage. A few minute. after•leaYing the gardens bre aght the party to the hall, now, alas, apparently given up to decay, for only one small room is furnished. The chapel, with its pretty reredos in blue and gold, and painted walls, woe owing to the damp showing signs of mould, but certainly the meet attractive portion was the large hall. The lower part is sixty-three yards long, oroamented with marble columns. each pair of a different colour, and were about six yards apart. The panels were hand painted in floral designs, whilst the floor was polished inlaid oak. A conservatory, from which we observed a solitary bat clinging to the roof, war tenantlem of its principal ornarnent—flowers, and the extensive parterre in the board the mansion was overgniwn with weeds Frotn the windows at the front a scene, lovely in the extieme, was presented to view. Overlooking the Mersey, it was one of those glorious English landecapeA never seen outside of the British Islands. Ten was laid at an hotel in Sutton village. after which the pun In strolled as far as the church, built by Mr. Naylor in honour of his lot.. wife. Then they went through the woofs, where they picked the rare Mayblaile Ilisfera nuatrt 1, with several orchids, wood-sanicle (macula cnneofnaol. with a few ferns; but nothing of any moment was gatherwl owing. probably, to the limited time. The field prizes for the natural order, nmen- eularrer, or buttercup family. was awarded to Mrs. Whit- taker and Miss Potter. The !Arty returned borne, pleaeed ' with the day's work by the eight o'clock train front Sutton • station.

div.p: PRIMITIVE MEIID)DISM IN WIDNES. LATINO THE MEMORIAL STONES OF A NEW

For some tirne past. n-M.Wlth;ianding the very indifferent state of trade in Whine., the members of the Primitive Methodist denomination have been steadily pursuing their purpose of taking up a position in the rapidly growing , neighbourhood lenownnr Simms Cross, at Widnes. The !freehold of the loknd sufficient for the pimp err of a school ' chapel has been bought, and the friends have decided to enter into a total expenditure of +Mout £llOO. Between £3OO and £4(O has been raised towanis this amonnt. The structure will be in the plain English style of architecture. will be 40 feet long by 30 feet broad, and at the end of it there will Ire la vestry 15 feet in length and 12 feet in breadth. Mr. Rim- ' met., of Widnes, is the architect. and the contractors' work will be carried out In, Mr. l'homes Sadler, of Widnen-rmid, in the sante town. The ceremony of laying the memorial stones took place on Saturday afternoon, in delightful weather, but the mutter of people to join the precession was far from being large. Probably this may be accounted for by the fact that 'he event, which ought to mark an era in the progress of the denomination in the town, was not advertised in a newspaper,—a few posters of nnt by any means large dimensions being ap- parently thoucht sufficient to afford all the publicity needed. The Revs. T Peters t Congregationalist), C. Hill- Rant end James Hutchinson (Wesleyan Methodists), F. Jeffs lot Frodshom), Thomas Wilshaw (of St. Helens), and J. Morton (of Runcorn). Were amongst throw who took part in the eeremnny. The Rev. W. Rowe, of Chester, general secretary of the Primitive Methodist Missions, delivered an address on connexional polity, and reviewed the progress of the denominmion from its very mai beginning,. Memorial stones were laid by thy following Elizabeth Annie ' Marshall,Miss Eliza Jane Drought, Miss Anne Hill, and Mi. Flossy Conon and the Rev. W. Malian., laitl a brick" ' at half It sokereign, Mr. David Wright one at a similar amount, and Mr. Wyles And Mr. Thomas Marshall a brick each at El. Under the fourth memorial stone was placed a sealed bottle. cnntaining a quarterly plan of the station, a copy of the Peinatvor Mrthaii,a, and the names of the trustees and the girl. who tool I ti.l the stones. At the conclusion of the ceremony tea was provided in the Hutchineon-street Chapel. A public meeting afterwards took place, at which Mr. John Drought presided. and most nf the ministers who took part in the ceremony delivered addresses. The laymen present included Messrs. D. Wright, James Deakin, Thos. Mamhall. Timm. Hughes, John Holloway, John Dale, Andrew Powl.on, Samuel Drought, J IV. Coxon, John Lea. Minslow, Thomas Hill, Wm, Pinches, and Samuel Pinches.

The lwar.c-ron or Num:ices (Mr. James Farrington) ' reported that ill comp' iAnce with instructions recrived, he had MAC another inspection with respect of the water supply of that portion of the township of Appleton, whielt includes ' Wilderepral, Stockton Heath, Birchdale, and Mill-lane, and : he begged to submit the following report, which in order , that the same might be more tangible he had divided it into four parts ,—Part I,oe that of Wilderspool, the length of , which is frost the first bridge on the m3in road leadintz horn ' Warrington to the Old Quay Canal Bridge, and from the Sarattens's HeAl to Tom Payne's Bridge. The total popula- tion is about 382 and the total number of house. 83. Out of this number, 24 houses, with a population of 100, are supplied with water from the Warrington Waterworks Com- pany mains. ro houses, with a population of 270, are cup. plied with water from pump wells, stored rain water, and an open well. There are 10 pump welle and one open one. The Water Company's mains are laid the entire length of the road from the first mentioned point to the second ; the cottages in the vicinity of the brewery are supplied with water both rot the mains and pomp; the water from the latter is considered to be very good. The maMs are not laid along the lOW leading to Tom Payne's Bridge beyond the brewery. The occupiers of nine cottages situate in thi. 1.0/01 have to obtain their water front an open well in a mall plantation on the bank of the river. It A within a few yards of the water, and at an ordinarily high tide the moil wm polluted with ttll kinds of filth from the river, and rendered quite on. fit for domestic purposes. All the 00, inhabitants of that line of road (with the exception of the occupier of one large house) receive their water from pump wells or stored rain water. The surroundings of some of the wells are not good, and considering the porous nature of the soil in the locality, aud their close proximity to the river and canal. Cr, open to be looked upon with a certain amount of sumielon. The water from one (after the well had been improved, and the water intercepted in sanitary pipes, with water-tight joints) haa been submittal for analysis, and returned a. being a acond-class water ore water of medium purity. Part 2nd. West portion, called Stockton Heath, comprising the length from the Old Quay Canal Midge to London Bridge. and from the Old Spade forge to the angle of She road near the Vimrage, including the mow, to Retl-lane Bridge. The total popul.ttinn of this part A about 841, end the total num- ber of houses 185. Oct of this number, 132 limas, contain. ing a population of 551, are supplied with water from the Water Company's mains. 80 housot, with a population of 382, are supplied horn pump wells and other saran There are in all 17 pumps. The company's mains are laid from the filet named pint to near lAndon bridge, anti alec from the forge to the angle mentioued, and along the road to near Red-lane bridge. 'The major part of the inhabitants in this melon Are supplied from the mains, and many others who at present fetch their water fronts considerAhle distance could be sitnilarly supplied. As stated by the Medical (lfficer, the National Schools, attended by 250 children, are without a reliable water supply. The arroundias and pneition of ante of the well. are not good. A sample front men well hail been analyeed, and certified as not being a water of the highest degree of purity, but still an ordinary good drinking water. The third part includes Birchdale and the Imam situate in the vicinity of London bridge. The population is abiut 88, and the number of houses about 22. The water is obtained from three pumps and the two open shallots wells. Nine cottages and one large loom in the road are supplied with water through the kindness of Mr. Robert Davies, in , allowing the ccupiers the use of the pump on his own pre- mises. The Inspector was of opinion that the ampany's , niains ehould be laid along the road, which would be a great boon 10 the residents. The fourth part is Mill- , lane and Altriuchannroad, which contain. 11 cottager and ; one large knee, and they are supplied from three pumps and one open ehallow well. He (the inspector) had received various complaints as to the quality of the water supplied bv the Warrington Water Works Company, but he was not prepared to substantiate such complaints, as he wm of opinion a great many of them were prompted through prejulice. It was decided that the Warrington Water Worke Com- pany should be written to anking whether they would be prep.:n.l to lay mains in those parts of Stockton Heath and Wilderspool where required ; that three samples of water should be obtained from the parts in question, and submit- ted for analyain; ..nd tlmt Mr. Farrington serve notices upon the owners of property which A without a water supply in thOAC cases where the maine were within 200 feet of such Property. This was all the business.

,1 'rim Midsummer Quarter Sessione of the Peace for the county of Chester enrolw enesl on Monday mooting, at the Castle of Chester: before Mr. Horatio Lloyd, deputy chair- man of quarter sessions, and a large attendance of magic- traten. The calendar contained the names of 15 prisoners, charged with 18 offences, all, with the exception of one of uttering counterfeit coin and two of unlawful wounding, of the ordinary trivial character. Toe CHRllOll.—The Chairman, in charging the grand , jury. said the calendar showed a very sensible Ilimioution in the crime in the county euring the past quarter, for while at the same 5,8160138 in 1879 the number of prisoners for trial at Chester ani Kingsford was 4(5, it was now only 31, a dirninution of one-third. Butt ere was one very umiak.- factory feature in the calendar, arid one which he was espe- cially sorry to observe, because for some time now he bad been congratulating grand jury after grand jury on the reverse of the picture now presented. In the present calendar there were no fewer than five juvenile offenders, whereas for a long time past there had not been a single ease of juvenile crime, and he had been in hopes that the action of reformatories and industrial schools one lieginning to make itself felt on the criminal clanses. and Ihor,tt,ore being n recruits to the ranks in juvenile offenders, and the calend ire being made up almost always of old offenders, they might look forward to the future hopefully, that we were gradually drifting into a better state of things. Perhaps it was no, and the presence of tine juvenile offenders in the calendar might be due to accidental circumstances, but as it stood it was an unsatisfactory feature, and they must coo- eider if anything could tie done to prevent its recurrence.
